Live Reporting
Edited by Jamie Whitehead and Manish Pandey, with technology reporters Tom Gerken, Shiona McCallum and Laura Cress
Microsoft restoring services after global outage causes disruption for millionspublished at 20:15 GMT
20:15 GMT
Jacob Phillips Live reporter
Image source, Reuters
Microsoft has apologised for a global outage that left
millions of users unable to access emails, it’s Teams messaging app or its AI
assistant, Co-Pilot - which were inaccessible in at least 70 countries.
The US tech giant blamed a "technical issue not related
to cyber or AI/agents" for the problem, saying it was introduced during an
"earlier network capacity upgrade".
In the UK the outage disrupted NHS England staff. But the
UK's cyber minister explained it did not affect 999 calls, front line NHS
111 services or cause transport disruption.
Hospital and rail passengers were affected in Canada while
court services and government offices in the US were also disrupted - both
countries are now slowly seeing operations return to normal.
Outage shows 'lack of resilience' in UK digital infrastructure - Commons committee chairpublished at 19:26 GMT
19:26 GMT
Image source, Getty Images
The Microsoft outage highlights the "lack of
resilience" in the UK's digital infrastructure, the chair of the House of
Commons science and technology committee says.
Chi Onwurah says the incident also shows the dangers such a
dependency can post to the country's security, economy and public services.
The committee previously published a report which stated the
UK's reliance on a small number of US-based providers for digital
infrastructure and public service delivery is a "strategic and economic
vulnerability".
The prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said a range of
services experienced disruptions today due to parts of government using
Microsoft services.
Disruption was also reported by the Welsh government, which
said it's "using contingency arrangements as needed".
In Northern Ireland, education and council services were interrupted,
with Belfast City Council saying there were issues "receiving and
responding" to emails.
And in Scotland, some systems were hit by the outage, with
the Scottish justice secretary telling the BBC the government's
"resilience operation" had been activated.
Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business
Charter, says it is a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely
on digital systems”.
"For many small and medium-sized enterprises, access to
email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and
suppliers to generating income," she says.
Artificial Intelligence strategist Walter Pasquarelli tells
the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the
outage puts "their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".
"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our
email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further,"
he says.
Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several
major tech companies, says what was unusual about this outage was the time it
took for Microsoft to recover. The resulting upset shows "our reliance on
a few large US corporations".
A spokesperson for Microsoft said "given the scale of
demand" it restored services gradually.
Any outage compensation likely to face hurdles, says UK lawyerpublished at 18:33 GMT
18:33 GMT
Tom Espiner Business reporter
Microsoft may face compensation claims over the Outlook
outage, but there would be lots of potential pitfalls for would-be claimants, a
lawyer says.
Whether an organisation or individual would stand a chance
of success in getting any compensation from Microsoft would depend on the
nature of the contract they have with the tech giant.
Customer terms, especially for free versions of Outlook, usually
specify that Microsoft is not liable for service interruptions, and courts
normally uphold these contracts if the terms are reasonable, says Riah Sattar,
a partner and head of dispute resolution at Thomas Mansfield Solicitors.
Businesses or individuals using paid-for versions of Outlook
are partly protected under the Consumer Rights Act in the UK, which says that paid-for
services must be delivered with reasonable care and skill.
However, the claimant would have to show that Microsoft was
liable for something it had control over, which is difficult to do.
The claimant would also have to show that the outage caused
them a loss.
'Hopefully it'll be a wake-up call': BBC readers react to Microsoft blackoutpublished at 18:07 GMT
18:07 GMT
As Microsoft systems continue to come back online following more than 20 hours of disruption, readers have been getting in touch with the BBC to describe their experiences.
It is fair to say some have had it better than others:
Wilber, London: "I’m exchanging the contract for my new home today. But since the email is not working, all the things [are] stuck and can’t move and we [have been] waiting this for a whole year!"
Callum, Ormskirk: "It's ridiculous that we've become so reliant on one company's products as a society that so many workplaces and educators are basically having to come to a standstill... hopefully it'll be a wake-up call"
Amar, Tanzania: "I'm in Zanzibar, Tanzania, where I'm working remotely, running my business. In the last 15 minutes, all the day's emails have come through... I spent the day reading on the beach, now it's time to catch up"
Microsoft outage had 'limited' impact on frontline services - UK cyber ministerpublished at 17:49 GMT
17:49 GMT
Image source, PA Media
Image caption,
Cyber minister Liz Lloyd has explained there has been "limited" impacts on frontline services
The UK cyber minister says the Microsoft outage has "mainly affected back-office functions such as messaging and email" and the government has seen "limited" reports of impact on frontline service delivery.
Liz Lloyd says 999 calls and NHS 111 services have been unaffected by the disruption and that HMRC and DWP phone lines are "fully operational" - although people may have had longer than usual waiting times.
She adds there has been no disruption to the transport network as a result of the outage.
Lloyd adds she has spoken to the CEO of Microsoft UK about their plans for a full return to normal services "as soon as possible".
She explains Microsoft is "seeing positive results".
"The government recognises this incident has been inconvenient and disruptive," she says.
"Affected departments and public sector organisations have plans in place for these events to mitigate potential impacts and continue their business operations."
Lloyd adds that the government will review the incident and use the lessons learnt to "inform our ongoing work to raise digital resilience across the UK".
Services beginning to resume in the US and Canadapublished at 17:28 GMT
17:28 GMT
Madeline Halpert Reporting from New York
Image source, Getty Images
Image caption,
Via Rail in Canada says despite the technical issues, services are running as normal
Earlier, we pointed to a number of entities that had been
impacted by the global outage.
Some of those affected are now seeing operations back to
normal, including the Arapahoe County Sheriff's Office in Colorado, which said
people being detained are now able to make bond payments online again.
Unity Health Toronto, which had said earlier that patients
and doctors may struggle to reach each other, says on their website that
"email services are gradually returning to normal as Microsoft works to
restore services".
Others, like several municipal governments in the US
impacted by the outage, had yet to provide an update on whether emails were
working again on Friday afternoon.
How the Microsoft 365 outage unfolded - a timelinepublished at 17:16 GMT
17:16 GMT
Tinshui Yeung Live reporter
Image source, Downdetector
Image caption,
Website Downdetector noted hundreds of reports on Thursday evening and Friday morning
All timestamps are in GMT, according to posts published on X.
12 November 17:54: Microsoft first acknowledges reports that users in the Americas are unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes.
18:07: Microsoft warns that the disruption may affect Microsoft 365 connectivity globally, not just in the Americas.
19:31: The company says an investigation found that a number of services had become “unexpectedly unavailable”, straining the remaining infrastructure.
19:50: Engineers start focusing on an issue that caused servers to fail automated health checks and become unavailable.
23:04: Microsoft says it’s returning some affected servers to service, and they “remain stable”.
13 November 00:06: Microsoft says servers returned to service can become unresponsive again once they receive traffic, and it is analysing the data to find out why.
04:36: After a series of efforts, Microsoft says it is seeing “partial recovery” in some regions.
09:24: “We’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue,” the company says.
13:32: The company says there are “broader improvements” in North America, “sustained improvements” across much of Europe and “encouraging recovery signals” in the Asia Pacific region.

"technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents".

says it is "deeply sorry" for the disruption and says it takes its
responsibilities "extremely seriously".
The statement explains: "The incident was introduced by
an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a
recent network change.
"We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to
restore service to remaining customers and regions."
Microsoft says it is restoring services gradually due to the
"scale of demand" and it will provide a full post-incident report
once its review is complete, the spokesperson adds.
Services slowly resuming after Microsoft outage impacts users around the worldpublished at 16:35 GMT
16:35 GMT

Image source, Getty Images
Microsoft services are slowly returning online after a
global outage impacted millions of users around the world.
What has happened?
Users
began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products
including Outlook and Teams on Thursday - these are programmes used by
more than 430 million people worldwide
Microsoft
said the disruption was
not caused by a cyber-security breach, and attributed the disruption
to "elevated load" on its infrastructure - although we still
don't know the specific cause yet
More than 20 hours after the issues began, the firm said "encouraging progress" was being seen and that email queues were "approaching normal levels"
While services are now returning online, that doesn't mean everything is working perfectly behind the scenes - expect some delayed emails for a while yet, writes BBC tech reporter Tom Gerken.
Despite the disruption, shares in Microsoft only dipped 0.2% in early trading after the US stock market opening, suggesting investors are not all that worried about what the outage.
Meanwhile, one cyber security expert has warned users to be
wary, telling the BBC cyber
criminals will likely capitalise on the disruption in an attempt to steal
sensitive data.

16:13 GMT

Image source, Getty Images
The exact words Microsoft is using are: "As of now, we
are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.”
This assessment might change of course.

but to get millions of people back online. So, any investigation into what
triggered this enormous outage can wait.

would “be here at this time on a Friday anyway,” one group of drinkers
confessed they would have been in the office had it not been for the Microsoft outage.

arrived at work as normal today, but had “given up” by late-morning as

others.

The committee previously published a report which stated the
UK's reliance on a small number of US-based providers for digital
infrastructure and public service delivery is a "strategic and economic

Microsoft may face compensation claims over the Outlook
outage, but there would be lots of potential pitfalls for would-be claimants, a
lawyer says.
Whether an organisation or individual would stand a chance
of success in getting any compensation from Microsoft would depend on the
nature of the contract they have with the tech giant.
Customer terms, especially for free versions of Outlook, usually
specify that Microsoft is not liable for service interruptions, and courts
normally uphold these contracts if the terms are reasonable, says Riah Sattar,
a partner and head of dispute resolution at Thomas Mansfield Solicitors.
Businesses or individuals using paid-for versions of Outlook
are partly protected under the Consumer Rights Act in the UK, which says that paid-for
services must be delivered with reasonable care and skill.
However, the claimant would have to show that Microsoft was
liable for something it had control over, which is difficult to do.
The claimant would also have to show that the outage caused
them a loss.

Amar, Tanzania: "I'm in Zanzibar, Tanzania, where I'm working remotely, running my business. In the last 15 minutes, all the day's emails have come through... I spent the day reading on the beach, now it's time to catch up"

"The government recognises this incident has been inconvenient and disruptive," she says.
"Affected departments and public sector organisations have plans in place for these events to mitigate potential impacts and continue their business operations."
Lloyd adds that the government will review the incident and use the lessons learnt to "inform our ongoing work to raise digital resilience across the UK".

articles.title: Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases
articles.body:
Perplexity Decider
How we train, evaluate, and use it.
We are releasing Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, the successors to our earlier decision models: v1, v1.1, v1.2, and Flash v1.2.
Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.
Perplexity Decider is inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI’s System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.
Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce locate, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.
In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.
What is a decision model?
A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:
- Yes / No: binary decisions.
- Multiple choice: custom multi-class labels.
- Score: ordered levels.
Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:
- Judging outputs: assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety.
- Routing: directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty.
- Moderation and security: detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs.
- Filtering and tagging: organizing large collections of content.
- Retrieval and reranking: scoring search results by relevance.
Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format.
Training
Turning a generative LLM into a decision model
We build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions.
For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special <|marker|> token indicates where to read out the model’s prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the question’s answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.
We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of  <|marker|> into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.
For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.
In v1.3, we introduce locate, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as “location” or an instruction such as “Extract the city name where the job is located.” The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list.
Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.
Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both ways
Our models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backbone’s full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.
Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:
- Everything sees everything (v1.2): The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked.
- Isolated questions (v1.3): The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable.
- Fully cacheable: The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.
We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.
Training recipe
Training proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on Qwen3.8-27B, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller Qwen3.5-4B model.
The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.
After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using LoRA. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backbone’s general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.
Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.
For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.
Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacher’s output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.
To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.
Adding the ability to extract information
The locate feature extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token, <|locate|>, a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider. 
We initialize  <|locate|> ’s embedding from <|marker|> learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own <|locate|> token.
The span head uses <|locate|> ’s representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the <|locate|> token’s representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.
We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.
We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.
Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the model’s outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.
Evaluation
We evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the Hugging Face Decision Index, Vals AI’s ClaimBench, and Artificial Analysis Decision Index.
Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites.
Internally, we built a suite of more than 200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Decider’s real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.
Query classification
At Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.
Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.
Domain-specific classification
We assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision models’ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).
For example, “judge the time complexity of a Python program”, or “use an annual financial report to determine whether a company’s unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve months”. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains.
Retrieval and Reranking
Search is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our models’ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.
We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each query–document pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points.
On the BEIR benchmark, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.
Multilingual classification
To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.
We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.
NER, PII and Extractive QA
We evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as “person” or “email address”, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.
We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.
We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflare’s Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each task’s primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category.
Image classification
Decider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.
Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.
Real-world decision requests
We sampled one million deduplicated, PII-masked requests submitted to the Perplexity Decision API during its first 18 days of availability. Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.
Production requests do not come with ground-truth labels, so we use frontier LLM judges to generate reference answers and measure each model’s agreement with them. We also group the requests into 10 task categories, including information extraction, domain classification, sentiment analysis, intent and routing, relevance ranking, content moderation, quality and compliance review, entity matching, business analysis, and an “Other” category. This breakdown shows how performance varies across real-world use cases.
The task mix is uneven: information extraction accounts for 425,402 questions, domain classification for 409,564, and sentiment analysis for 344,158. Together, these three categories make up 50.8% of the sampled questions.
Decider v1.3 achieves the highest agreement with the judges at 93.98%, compared with 93.68% for Decider v1.2 and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Decider v1.3 and Jev 1.14 are closely matched on domain classification and sentiment analysis, with gaps of 0.34 and 0.07 percentage points, respectively. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking, while Decider v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction (the most common task in the sample) and by 1.21 points on intent and routing.
The chart below compares the reported cost of running the same one million production requests. Each request can contain multiple questions, so the unit here is requests, not individual questions.
Robustness
We evaluated label sensitivity on 372 multiple-choice questions, making 4,788 requests per model. We reordered options, reassigned labels to answer texts, and renamed labels while preserving each question’s meaning, then checked whether the model’s semantic answer changed. Lower flip rates indicate greater stability.
Decider v1.3 changed its answer on just 0.27% of questions under each transformation, compared with 2.69–4.84% for Jev 1.14. We also repeated identical inputs to measure serving variability: Decider v1.3 showed no changes, while Jev 1.14 changed on 1.88% of questions.
How we use Decider
Decider is built for workflows that need fast and structured decisions. In this section we explore how to leverage them to produce meaningful impact on the way we work. Here are some that stood out.
Self-improving security rules
Internally, we are already using Decider to improve our security policies.
The activity of our agents is recorded and a series of rule-based checks are performed to identify any problematic behavior. A rule-based approach means that we can monitor our agents in real-time with negligible latency added. Offline, we use Decider to look at samples from these recorded agent logs. In the case that no problematic behavior was flagged, Decider checks if there is something that our set of rules missed; and in the case that an alarm was raised, Decider checks whether this was a false alarm. Any records where our rule set fails in either case are sent to an agent for triage and a fix to the rules is proposed, to be approved by a member of our security team.
In one day, Decider read 1 billion tokens across 7,000 agent sessions and identified flaws that led to 14 rule fixes, 6 of which were approved and shipped within two days. Replayed on a week of logs, the fixes cut our busiest rule's volume by 52%, and the widened rules caught about 40% more legitimate actions to investigate.
Monitoring RL rollouts
When we post-train models with reinforcement learning, aggregate metrics such as a terminal reward do not explain why a rollout (an individual attempt at a task) succeeded or failed. It can lose reward unfairly because a tool service or the sandbox failed, or receive undeserved reward if the evaluator overlooks an unsupported claim, such as a made-up value that no tool returned.
We use Decider to monitor rollouts for these cases. Code first identifies parts of a rollout that warrant closer inspection: a failed tool call and the surrounding reasoning, code that ran without errors, or the final answer. Decider then answers multiple-choice questions about each part, such as what failed in a step (a tool service, an external site, the sandbox, the harness, or the agent’s own code) and whether the agent interpreted the result correctly. We bundle all questions about a given part into a single request and store the probabilities rather than a verdict, so we can adjust thresholds later without querying Decider again. The monitor only observes and diagnoses: it never changes a reward or stops a run.
Page quality filtering
When crawling web pages to index and serve to users, many pages are too low quality to be of any use. This includes anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs, and error pages, as well as correctly loaded web pages that just don’t contain any helpful information, such as spam, SEO filler or navigation-only pages. These low-quality pages need to be identified and filtered out of our index.
Using Decider, we can judge the quality of pages as we crawl them. In the same forward pass, we perform a suite of other classification tasks such as identifying the domain and intended audience of the content and whether it contains harmful, illegal, or personally identifiable information. Compared to using an LLM judge, Decider is considerably faster and cheaper.
Beyond these internal uses, Decider also fits workflows such as the following.
Visual QA
Because Decider reads images, it also works as a visual checker, reviewing style changes to web pages or apps and identifying faults. It can review page screenshots for clipped text, overlapping elements, broken layouts before a change ships, or flag charts whose design could mislead a reader or break a brand guide.
Browser navigation
Agents can use Decider for the small decisions inside larger tasks. A browser agent can send a screenshot at each step and receive detailed information about the state of the page and the expected outcome of each possible action.
Planning research tasks
Users’ questions can greatly vary in their complexity, as does the depth of search that needs to be performed to find an answer. Decider can estimate this before search begins, allowing for fewer resources to be spent on simple questions.
Getting started
Decider returns probabilities. The appropriate decision threshold depends on the application. Label frequencies and the relative costs of false positives and false negatives vary across use cases. We therefore encourage users to tune thresholds on a small, representative labeled development set rather than assume that a fixed cutoff will work equally well across tasks.
We recommend using Decider v1.3 for nuanced judgments, detailed rubrics, and workflows where errors are costly. Choose Decider Flash v1.3 for high-volume routing, labeling, and filtering where latency and cost are the main constraints. Evaluate both models on representative examples from your workload, then choose the model that meets your quality, latency, and budget requirements.
Both models are available as downloadable weights on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.

articles.title: Is there a 'right amount' of AI?
articles.body:
Gonna go have a panic attack now.
Is there a ‘right amount’ of AI?
While I’ve made my skepticism of AI clear by now, I’m not an anti-AI purist fighting against “no apps with any hint of AI coding allowed on my machine.” For one thing, it’s almost certainly a lost battle. Microsoft and Apple are both using coding agents for OS development, and while I can’t prove that most people running Linux have at least some LLM-touched code somewhere on their system, I’d be incredibly surprised if it’s not there.
Just this week, I moved back to Overcast from Castro as my podcast player. (I’ve spent a decade or so switching between them. Castro’s queue system is terrific, but the app has always been buggier than Overcast, its subscription price skyrocketed a year or so ago, and it’s now on its third owner—a shady-looking company that’s already diluted the privacy policy.) I know that developer Marco Arment has become an enthusiastic “agentic coder”, and that this means Overcast has Claude-generated code in it. Ditto his fun new app Fineliner, which I’m using on my new iPad mini (more about which later). I don’t think either of these programs are going to erase my data, make my iPad overheat, or send my credit card information to Russian hackers. In theory, what Lex Friedman wrote recently on the subject of vibe-coding, well, vibes with me:
AI has dramatically reduced the cost of producing an app, but it hasn’t reduced the work required to produce a great app. There’s a difference between generating something that works and something that works reliably, handles unexpected situations, feels intuitive, respects platform conventions, and continues improving. […] I will gladly pay for apps that feel crafted. I want apps that show refinement, testing, and thoughtfulness. I want apps from developers I trust will keep on building and iterating. I want apps from developers who feel invested—those are the ones I’m willing, even eager, to invest in.
(Note that’s Lex Friedman, who is cool, not Lex Fridman, who sucks.) And, yes, I think Marco is a developer who feels invested. He shows deep concern for code quality, to the point where he rather (in)famously eschewed using existing libraries for functions he could code himself. He wanted to understand his code inside and out.
So. Let’s talk about Big Walk.
If you haven’t heard of it, Big Walk is a game from House House, the Untitled Goose Game people, published by technically-still-Mac-developers Panic. It was a favorite for this year’s Independent Games Festival awards, but a group of IGF jurists issued a statement declaring they would “decline to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.” They specifically refused to make a distinction between using genAI for assets (e.g., graphics and sound) and code, writing,
Programming is a creative discipline whose labour deserves the same respect we extend to any part of making a game. This extends to the past work used to train these models without the creators’ consent.
This led House House to confess that, okay, they “sparingly” used LLMs to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs”. Less than a percent of a percent of the code in Big Walk was touched in any way by LLMs, and they went out of their way to say “this is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” and that they “support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”
Based on everything above, I shouldn’t have any issue with this. And at first, I didn’t. It all struck me as a tempest in a (Utah) teapot.
But then I read this.
House House, an already very successful studio with not insignificant resources, made a real choice to rely on a morally abhorrent software system rather than engage the help of real people—whether in the form of paid contracting or just friendly help. I want to say this not to try to exaggerate the scope of what they did but to make it absolutely clear that there is a real, material dimension to this, even if some want to characterize this issue as a purely abstract test of ritual purity.
You may balk at “morally abhorrent software system,” but Bruno Dias (the blog post author) is not wrong when he writes “to use LLMs is to willingly participate in a noxious political project and to use the product of exploitative and morally unacceptable processes.” I wrote about that in “AI’s Chicken Sandwich Problem”; in short form, LLMs do not exist in a vacuum. As he continues,
I’m not going to try to argue that any and all LLM usage is equally bad, but either an ethical boundary exists or it doesn’t. There are some ethical faults we generally expect people to not be 100% compliant with, of course, but there are some ethical faults we think it’s reasonable to expect people to never breach without sanction. I think using a completely optional set of highly subsidized SaaS products that did not exist two years ago is in the latter set.
If you disagree, perhaps stop to think about how heavily you’ve been propagandized and how much you’ve mentally surrendered to the normalization of these systems. It is very possible to do things without using an LLM, even things that are hard; and if anything, one of the harms of the “AI” political project is the propaganda machine dedicated to making you feel stupid and helpless.
And, you know, this is something that concerns me.
I recently wrote, “I think I’d lose something meaningful, something vital, if I couldn’t understand the code [that I’ve written]—to be able to read it line by line and know what each API call does, why certain choices are better than others, how it all comes together.” While I’m not suggesting that everyone who goes whole hog for agentic coding is doomed to lose the ability to understand their own code, there’s increasing evidence that “de-skilling” is a real issue, as well as evidence that the more leeway you give coding agents the worse your codebase is likely to get. Anecdotal tales of discovering Claude has written four versions of the same function in different places, finding giant sections of code that never get called, and “bug-finding” agents that imagine and even create bugs are growing rampant. LLMs and agents appear to “know” your codebase inside and out, but they don’t actually understand anything other than statistical relationships between words and phrases in specific contexts. The LLMs themselves don’t even “know” they’re working with code.
When I listen to Accidental Tech Podcast and hear Arment getting so enthusiastic about coding agents, I admit I have trouble reconciling “I don’t like using libraries I haven’t written” with “I love having robots write code for me”. Sure, it’s absolutely possible for a human to check every bit of LLM-generated code; I have little doubt that the code in Big Walk is code House House fully understands. A lot of LLM-contributed code I’ve seen is short, clear fixes and improvements, absurd to point to as poisonous, incomprehensible slop. Reining in your agents flips the complaint in the last paragraph around: the less LLM-generated code you use, the easier that code is to vet.
The larger point here, though, isn’t about Big Walk, or Overcast, or how many long-standing minor bugs in macOS Claude fixed (or how many brand new minor bugs in macOS Claude may have introduced). It’s about treating AI-assisted coding as something that must be used now that it’s here, whether we see it as an unalloyed good or as a tool whose benefits outweigh its drawbacks, or even as an unavoidable evil. It is, as Dias writes, very possible to do things without using an LLM, even things that are hard.
One could use LLMs for coding in a limited, intentional way, and the language models we have now are mostly trained on open-source, publicly-available code, making them (arguably) less objectionable than generating images or music or annoying emails pitching vibe-coded Markdown viewers. But mostly does heavy lifting in that sentence—and even if the code is open source, that doesn’t mean it’s legal to train on. If Claude inadvertently incorporates a meaningful chunk of GPL-licensed code in your non-GPL software, you have a problem. I suspect this is a problem that already exists in thousands of codebases.
We can envision a future that solves the big problems with LLM-assisted coding. The models run locally, not in data centers that convert electricity and water into money funneled to Elon Musk and Sam Altman; the training corpus only contains code whose license allows training. I suspect any open source license that allows commercial reuse falls into this category, unless one adds an explicit “no AI” clause. That future could be right around the corner. But we have to deal with the LLMs we have, not the LLMs we wish for.
So…where does that leave me? Back where I started, I suppose. It’s practical for me to swear off LLMs for my work, but not practical to avoid it in every piece of software that I use. But I think it’s something that indie developers in particular should be more wary of than what I’m seeing in the community. As I was finishing this article up this morning, this post came across my Mastodon timeline, from the head of the venerable indie design/coding outfit Iconfactory:
And, you know, yeah, I get that. I can no longer make a living doing technical writing because of AI, and AI is bad at technical writing in precisely the same way it’s bad at everything: good enough to slide by if you don’t really care. It’s more than a little concerning that otherwise perceptive people don’t understand that the same issues that plague those AI-generated posters at their local brewpub apply to everything AI-generated, and everything includes code.
I’m not saying you can’t use generative AI in the creation of terrific apps; IGF award arguments aside, Big Walk seems to qualify. But LLMs, by definition, can’t make anything thoughtfully, because LLMs have no thoughts. Everything Lex wants—apps that feel crafted, that show refinement, that feel intuitive—requires a human developer not only with taste, but with understanding. And the more you delegate to your robot coding assistant, the less you understand. Again, the less LLM-generated code you use, the easier that code is to vet. And the least amount of LLM-generated code you can use is always zero.
To support my writing, throw me a tip on Ko-fi.com!

articles.title: Meta discussed attacking Jonathan Haidt — now even his haters are annoyed
articles.body:
Three years ago, Meta apparently considered a plan to turn public opinion against one of its most influential opponents, Jonathan Haidt. But since the proposal was revealed in court filings last month, it’s backfired. In fact, if there’s one thing Anxious Generation author Haidt and his critics can agree on, it’s being mad at Meta.
Meta discussed attacking Jonathan Haidt — now even his haters are annoyed
Meta has ticked off academics on all sides of the social media and mental health debate.
Recent court filings in California revealed that Meta employees had discussed in 2023 a “Whisper strategy” to “turn academics against Haidt,” who would soon publish a bestselling book arguing that platforms like Meta’s were hurting kids. Haidt had spent years popularizing his theory that social media and smartphones are to blame for the decline in teens’ mental health, including in his 2018 book The Coddling of the American Mind and before Congress in 2022. To counter it, Meta apparently considered a “Below-the-line campaign,” including one idea to “Get Gellman to write a take-down piece” — possibly a reference to Columbia University statistics and political science professor Andrew Gelman, who’d previously publicly critiqued Haidt, though the spelling differs.
Meta employees had discussed in 2023 a “Whisper strategy” to “turn academics against Haidt”
It’s unclear if Meta ever acted on the strategy those employees appeared to consider. But the revelation has stirred up a much louder backlash among both Haidt and his most prominent detractors, most of whom weren’t mentioned by name. Meta declined to comment for this article.
Several academics have come forward to insist Meta had no hand in their opposition to Haidt. “No. I was not paid to critique the Anxious Generation. I came to the conclusion that the science featured in it was flawed all on my own,” reads the title of a Substack post from Candice Odgers, a prominent psychology professor who studies the effects of tech on teens and has frequently critiqued Haidt’s work. “I have never been approached by Meta to shape what I say publicly about the research on adolescents and social media,” Odgers wrote. “My views are my own, and are grounded in the years of research I’ve done on this topic.”
“No. I was not paid to critique the Anxious Generation”
“These days, I have absolutely nothing nice to say about Meta-the-company despite knowing a few amazing people who work there. I think the company is unethical to the core,” wrote danah boyd, a communication professor at Cornell University who has studied how teens use social media. “But I still stand by my research on teens and the research of others who have done rigorous analyses putting teens’ lives into context.”
Haidt is an extremely influential but polarizing figure. Through his bestselling book, The Anxious Generation, and related writing, he has made the case that social media and smartphone access for kids has contributed to a significant decline in mental health. His work has found support among academics including frequent collaborator and San Diego State University psychology professor Jean Twenge, and Haidt has published responses to the debate over his findings. But other longtime researchers in the field say the available evidence does not ultimately support his theory, and social media’s impact on teens at the population level is at most mixed.
Though Gelman has previously critiqued Haidt’s methods, this time he came to his defense, denouncing Meta’s private discussions. “I think it’s horrible for Haidt that this happened to him,” Gelman told The Verge in an interview. He wrote on his blog that he’s “never been contacted by anyone at Facebook or Meta regarding Jonathan Haidt or his work.” While he said he has received money from the company in the past, including a $25,000 “no-strings-attached donation” in 2016 through Columbia for his research, the money has never been related to “social media’s impact on teen health.”
Gelman says that Meta has every right to be in the conversation on the topic — but it should do so openly. “Doing it behind the scenes, it’s creepy. It’s horrible. I have nothing good to say about that,” he said.
“The idea that Meta would create a whisper campaign or whatever against any scholar is gross”
“The idea that Meta would create a whisper campaign or whatever against any scholar is gross,” said Chris Ferguson, a Stetson University psychology professor, in an email to The Verge. Ferguson published a meta-analysis of experimental studies on social media’s impact on mental health that found limited evidence of a causal effect. Ferguson, who said he receives “no funding from Meta or any other tech company,” accused both Haidt and Meta of being “more similar than different.”
“Both have been aggressive, and a pernicious influence on our understanding of youth mental health,” Ferguson wrote, saying that Haidt’s viewpoint is not backed up by science. “It’s possible to view Meta as a big, ugly, cynical, unethical company and, at the same time, view Jonathan Haidt as a pseudoscientist who should know better [than] to peddle nonsense capitalizing on parental fears for profit.”
The Meta meeting notes were disclosed on a court docket for a group of consolidated lawsuits against Meta and other social media companies alleging they misled the public about their services’ safety risks to teens. Meta has recently faced several high-profile legal defeats in similar cases that could cost it billions in penalties, and separately settled claims from state attorneys general for $17.1 billion.
In a statement to The Verge, Haidt said he’s never suggested the researchers named in this article were paid by Meta to critique his work, and hasn’t seen evidence to suggest that. “As a social psychologist who has studied the benefits of viewpoint diversity, I welcome opposing views and civil, rigorous scientific debate. Criticism by these researchers has caused me and my research group to dig deeper and sharpen our arguments,” Haidt says, noting that his research group has published “multiple review papers” laying out evidence that heavy social media use is harmful.
“I am glad to see that so many social scientists are expressing strong criticism of Meta”
“Meta’s own internal studies confirm our finding. Meta’s internal documents also show that the company discussed a plan to distort the academic debate and process, a tactic straight out of the Big Tobacco playbook,” Haidt added. “That should concern anyone who cares about scientific integrity and the well-being of children. I am glad to see that so many social scientists are expressing strong criticism of Meta for doing so.”
Ferguson said it’s not healthy for science to be associated with any one individual, and that Haidt himself could do more to discourage that. “I think people are slowly realizing it’s possible both to believe that Meta is evil and Haidt is full of crap at the same time,” Ferguson said.

articles.title: The Dawn of the Data Intelligence Engineer
articles.body:
I asked Nick Ursa, our lead data engineer (and MotherDuck co-founder), how AI had changed his job. His answer: "This is the first time in my career with no backlog."
You'd think that would leave him with plenty of time on his hands, but he's busier than ever. While the backlog is gone, the answers still have to be right, and a human still has to decide how much quality control to do. Whereas once upon a time his job was to make sure the numbers he was computing were right, now his job is to make sure that the numbers that an LLM or agent comes up with are right.
That's a different job from working a ticket queue. At Data Outpost on November 4, I proposed a name for this new role: the Data Intelligence Engineer. I think it's now the emergent role on an AI-enabled data team, and I’d like to share why.
What a data team is for?
A data team has one job: enable the business to make good decisions. The faster they can make those decisions, based on a more accurate picture of what is happening, the better those decisions can be.
The hard part has been the route a question takes to become an answer. It moves like a relay. A marketing leader comes into work on Monday and notices that there was a spike in churn over the last week. Why did that happen? They file a ticket with the data team to investigate. An analyst picks up the ticket, and as they dig in, they realize some key data is not exported from one of the data sources. They file a ticket to ask a data engineer to look into it. That needs a change in one of the data pipelines, so the data engineer makes the change, tests it, runs the backfill, tests the backfill, and resolves the ticket. Then the ball is back in the court of the analyst, who can build the dashboard that was needed. By the time it ships, the marketing person can no longer remember why they asked in the first place. The churn rate recovered a couple of weeks later on its own.
This isn’t calling anyone out as not operating effectively or urgently; nobody in that relay did anything wrong. But every handoff means waiting, context is lost, and the half-life of the ability to effectively act on the answer to the question slowly decays.
As an aside, we should note that there was a whole generation of AI enabled tools that didn’t really help; the co-pilot era made some of the turnarounds faster, but the problem was that there were too many handoffs to be able to act quickly enough.
Something is different this time
Before December 2025, the case against AI for analytics was easy to make. LLMs wrote bad SQL. Business logic was unknowable. The sensible conclusion was that this was never going to work. In fact, I used to talk about how data teams were more or less exempt from the disruption that was happening in other areas of software.
Then, all of a sudden, the ground moved. New models got better at SQL. Business logic turned out to be something an agent can figure out with some helpful context. And agents went multi-turn, which means they don't have to get it right the first time. They can try a query, look at what came back, and try again, just like a human analyst would do. Put those together and it … just … works.
Self-service BI has been right around the corner for decades, what makes this different? Well, as a bit of an existence proof, here’s an example; the presentation I gave at Data Outpost was not created as a powerpoint deck or Google Slides, it was an app that I built using MotherDuck and Claude. I used live datasets from four different data sources, built a number of interactive and animated visualizations. Anything I did could be done by virtually anyone; I didn’t look at a single line of code or SQL.
It is important to stress that this isn’t just a way to automate building your dashboards. BI is typically pretty static, with maybe a couple of drill-downs. But with AI, you can build much richer visualizations. And what’s more, if you can build a dashboard with a prompt, you can go beyond that and also build a full-blown app.
Allowing business stakeholders to answer questions with data on their own has an even broader benefit than just shortening the data team’s backlog; it actually allows them to make better decisions. By cutting down the amount of time it takes and the number of handoffs involved, they can ask more questions. They can ask follow up questions while they still have all of the context in their heads. This means they can make confident decisions faster.
Which of these jobs can be a prompt?
AI is dramatically changing the job information workers perform. Software engineers often find their time being spent babysitting Claude sessions and rubber stamping agent-written code. What about the traditional roles of the data team? Which of their jobs, to put it a bit provocatively, can be a prompt?
As uncomfortable as the answer might be, rather a lot can be done via a prompt. In the not too distant future, writing SQL queries, creating dashboards, and building dbt pipelines are not going to be things that require specialized knowledge to do. Agents are likely better than humans at these tasks already, and they’re only going to get better. Our Data Engineer, Nick, moved us from one version of Airflow to another in a weekend, with minimal supervision, which once would have taken a week.
Writing code or SQL or building dashboards was never the whole job, though. The need for accurate data and the ability to understand it doesn’t go away. And someone has to be accountable, who can sign off and say “yes, this is right”. That takes a human in the loop. Quoth Nick, one more time, “Data eng, regardless of tooling or who does it, is an accountability function."
What still needs a human
Once agents are writing the code, what’s left in the data world? It turns out quite a lot. Humans need to make sure that other stakeholders without the word “Data” in their title are able to solve problems with data. That means they need to ensure a clean data model with appropriate context and annotations, a clear ontology to ensure that terms and concepts are being applied consistently throughout, and also they need to make sure that things continue to work.
These aren’t things that a model can intuit from data or history.  A model knows SQL. It doesn't know how your company counts revenue, or which of several similar-looking tables is the real one (it is revenue_cpx_new_revised_v2_use_this_one ) . A model doesn’t know that when the sales team talks about revenue they mean commissionable revenue, and the finance team uses something different.
Context is a crutch that is difficult to maintain. What’s even better is just building a clean data model in the first place. There is a good analogy with software; I tend to consider it a user experience failure any time your user has to read the manual; a cleaner design would have made whatever they were trying to do obvious. Context is just a manual for agents; if you can make the data model simple and clear enough, it can save them a lot of time and energy (and tokens).
Meet the Data Intelligence Engineer
The jobs to be done for a data person in the age of AI don’t really match any of the typical responsibilities of other data team members. I think it is different enough to merit a new title, which I hereby dub the “Data Intelligence Engineer”
The Data Intelligence Engineer automates the data engineer's work (ingestion) and the analytics engineer's work (transformation and modeling) by creating and conducting software agents. They encode their knowledge of the system into shared context that can be used by other agents to answer questions about the organization. These include things like which fields are joinable but also what someone in the company means when they say “ARR”.
Evals are another big part of their responsibility; these are the system tests that validate that when you ask questions with a known answer, the answer is correct. A good eval suite can give confidence that the types of questions that users ask of the system are going to be answered correctly by the agent. Evals also are a way of knowing when something breaks.
The goal of a Data Intelligence Engineer is to enable self-service. That is, anyone in the organization should be able to open Claude or ChatGPT or another agent and answer questions correctly about the business, use that to build apps and visualizations, and in the end, make high quality decisions with the benefit of data. . When the Data Intelligence Engineer does the job well, everyone who asks a question gets the experience of working with the smartest analyst in the company.
Day to day, that means they are going to be building frameworks, building the data model, curating the context, preventing things from getting broken, fixing them when they break anyway, running evals, and being accountable for the surfaces the business depends on. We wrote the whole thing up as a job description, because we believe this is the way things are going and it's time to give it a name.
If you're a data engineer, an analytics engineer, or an analyst, you'll recognize parts of this. Those roles were already blending into each other, and morphing into something new. This is a role you play, whatever your title says.
Won't this be chaos?
It's a fair question. More people building means more chances to be wrong, with less oversight. There is the possibility of making stupendously silly mistakes by acting on the wrong data. I’ll leave it up to the reader whether they think that stupendously silly mistakes are something new or not. The scary thing is that now the data team can be held responsible for them.
There are two things that help. The first is that the closer you are to the problem, the better you can spot errors. The person who lives with the churn number notices when it looks off. From experience, we’ve found that results actually improve because the business owner has a fingertip feel on their area; they know when something isn’t right, and can often spot problems even in the source data.
The other thing that helps is that you don’t need to watch everything with the same level of vigilance. Another quotable quote from our friend Nick is that “Agents need supervision proportional to their blast radius." That is, if something is going to be used for important reporting or decisions, you should pay a lot of attention. If you’re trying to figure out how many sandwiches to order for lunch, it probably isn’t going to cause a riot if you order too many with habanero mustard because Claude imagines it is extra tasty.
You can think of this in three circles of supervision. The outer is the Wild West. Anyone can build, they hopefully build on a reasonable foundation, but the data team keeps their hands off. The next tier is the Curated set. This is a set of dashboards, visualizations, apps, and metrics that is important to the business in some form or another. When something breaks in these dashboards, the data team should make a best effort to fix them. Finally there is the inner circle, the Core. This contains key metrics for the organization, things that are important to get right. The data team should make sure that these are high quality and predictable at all times. The board number lives in the Core.
What does this all have to do with MotherDuck?
On MotherDuck, we build mechanisms to empower your AI enabled data team. Flights are vibe-codable pipelines that can pull data into your warehouse and translate it into a sane model. Context lives in Guides, which are markdown files describing your data model and your business. A Guide starts out as private, but an admin can promote it to apply to the whole organization so that every person and agent works from the same definitions. We call the data visualizations that can be created by agents “Dives”. Every person and agent gets its own Duckling, a dedicated DuckDB instance. All of these are reachable from SQL, so one person or agent can work a problem across ingestion, transformation, context, and apps without a handoff between tools.
The only way out is through
We're in a chaotic moment. Chaos breeds the biggest opportunities, and the tools hand you some real super-powers if you're willing to pick them up. We're all learning how to do this together.
The data team isn't going anywhere. Someone still has to own the data model, curate the context, keep things working, and answer for the results. No-backlog-Nick has more to do than ever, and but the job is changing and not going back.
So who's doing this at your company, and what do you call them?
PS - if you want to see my slides from the talk, check out the Dive Gallery
