articles.title: Technology as a Search Problem
articles.body:
One of my ongoing research interests is understanding the nature of technological progress: How does new technology come into the world and improve over time? What sort of factors affect it? How, in general, should we think about it? I’ve come at this question from a few different angles: posts looking at the operations and legacy of Bell Labs, posts looking at how specific technologies improved over time, posts looking at how frequent multiple invention is and how long we wait for new inventions, and so on.
My current line of thinking is that creating some new technology is best thought of as a search process. A given technology can be thought of as a point in some high-dimensional “design space” or “technology space,” which contains every possible technology: every conceivable arrangement of parts, materials, natural phenomena, and so on. The job of the would-be inventor is to navigate this space, sifting through the arrangements of elements that don’t work to find the ones that will.
This search process is made difficult by the fact that, as with any situation where you’re enumerating the possible combinations of a large number of elements, technology space is incomprehensibly vast. In “Are Technologies Inevitable?” economist Matt Clancy notes that Wikipedia listed 272 “named equations” that describe various regularities in the world, ranging from the Navier-Stokes equations (which describe the motion of fluids) to the Arrhenius equation (which describes chemical reaction rates as a function of temperature) to the Exner equation (which describes how sediment gets deposited in a river). If we use this as a (very rough) estimate as to the number of different phenomena that a technology can leverage, it implies an enormous number of possible technologies that could be created. As Clancy writes:
If we’ve got 272 regularities to work with, for example, then the number of possible combinations of these regularities is two, raised to the power of 272 (since every regularity can be used or not used: two options). But 2^272 is more than some estimates of the number of atoms in the observable universe. And that’s got to be an undercount of the number of possible technologies, since it counts all technologies that use the same principles together as the same thing, even if they orchestrate them in vastly different ways or use them in vastly different magnitudes.
By comparison, the most common estimate for the number of atoms in the universe is around 10^80, or ~2^265. And it’s likely there are many, many more regularities that some technology could harness than 272. (Some in-progress work on this that I haven’t yet completed suggests that there are at least thousands.)
And as Clancy notes, this outrageously huge number dramatically undercounts the number of possible technologies, because it doesn’t take into account that the same phenomena can be used in lots of different ways. In Brian Arthur and Wolfgang Polak’s paper “The Evolution of Technology within a Simple Computer Model” (which we looked at earlier this year), Arthur and Polak note that even within the universe of logic circuits made up of three basic elements (the NAND gate and the values of 1 and 0), the number of different circuits you can make for even a small number of inputs and outputs is staggeringly large:
The emergence of circuits such as 8-bit adders seems not difficult. But consider the combinatorics. If a component has n inputs and m outputs there are (2^m)^(2^n) possible phenotypes, each of which could be realized in a practical way by a large number of different circuits. For example, an 8-bit adder is one of over 10^177,554 phenotypes with 16 inputs and 9 outputs.
So the search space for some new technology is vast. And the way that we tackle vast search spaces is with information. Each bit of information cuts a search space in half, so even a relatively small amount of information can quickly narrow down what seems like a huge search space. When we create some new technology, what we’re doing is gathering information: figuring out what will work and what won’t work, what’s promising and what isn’t, narrowing down the huge space of technological possibilities and finding something within it that accomplishes some particular goal.
In the 19th century, for instance, many people were interested in building a mechanical flying machine, but it wasn’t clear the exact arrangement of elements that would yield a successful one. Thanks to knowledge of the laws of physics, and an existence proof of birds, would-be inventors were already working within a considerably narrowed search space: they knew roughly what elements a flying machine would need to have — lifting surfaces, a propulsion system, and a means of control — and had a general idea of how they should be arranged. But there were a huge number of ways that you could build a flying machine from these basic elements, and people spent a great deal of time and effort building different sorts of machines that did not in fact work. The Wright brothers’ eventual success can in large part be attributed to the fact that they were exceptionally talented at gathering information, enabling them to converge on a working airplane design far faster than their competitors.
I previously explored the nature of technological search in that previous piece looking at Arthur and Polak technological evolution paper, which uses a simple simulation to evolve different logic circuits, finding workable technologies amidst an enormous sea of possibilities. I really liked the basic simulation method Arthur used in this paper — randomly generating technologies to see how easy or hard it was to find working ones — and wanted to use simulation myself to further explore the dynamics of technological search. But while Arthur uses digital circuits — different arrangements of logic gates like NAND, OR, AND, etc. that can perform functions like addition — I wanted a more general model that could capture the nature of many different types of technology, while still being simple enough to simulate easily.
The PTOP model
The model I came up with is inspired by another of Brian Arthur’s examinations of the nature of technology: his book The Nature of Technology. In this book Arthur describes technology as fundamentally “a set of phenomena captured and put to use.” He writes that:
… a practical technology consists of many phenomena working together. A radio receiver is not just a collection of parts. Nor is it merely a miniature signal processing factory. It is the orchestration of a collection of phenomena — induction, electron attraction and repulsion, electron emission, voltage drop across resistance, frequency resonance — all convened and set up to work in concert for a specific purpose.
Edison’s lightbulb, for instance, took advantage of several different phenomena: Joule heating, the phenomenon that electric current running through a material will raise its temperature. Incandescence, the phenomenon that a hot enough object will emit light. Transparency, the phenomenon that certain materials will allow the passage of light. And so on.
Phenomena like this are typically triggered automatically when the right conditions are created, which you can think about as being when the right objects, with the right properties, are placed in some particular arrangement. In the lightbulb, Joule heating occurs automatically when electric current runs through the filament, and incandescence occurs automatically when the filament gets hot enough. And the bulb had a vacuum atmosphere to prevent another, unwanted phenomenon — carbon reacting with oxygen — automatically occurring and destroying the carbon filament.
These three elements — Phenomena, Objects, and Properties — are the basic components of the technological model I came up with, which I call PTOP, for Phenomena Triggered by Objects with Properties. In this model you have some collection of objects, which can have some specified set of properties. Whenever the right objects with the right properties are placed in the proper arrangement, a phenomenon will be automatically triggered, which can have various effects: modifying the properties of existing objects, creating new objects, and so on. By chaining the correct objects and phenomena together in the correct order, you can create your desired outcome, which is some particular object or objects with some specific set of desirable properties. A simple, conceptual PTOP model for the lightbulb, for instance, might look like this:
By arranging the right sort of filament, an atmosphere, a bulb container, and electric current, you can trigger a series of phenomena that will ultimately result in the creation of light with desirable properties.
And here’s a sketch of a PTOP model for a more complicated technology, a Xerox machine, which uses various phenomena such as “photoconductivity” and “corona discharge” to generate a copy of a document:
I like this model because it captures the basic elements — natural phenomena and the conditions that trigger them — inherent to all types of technology, such that we can study the ‘space’ of possible technologies. And you can implement the basic idea in many different ways, from very simple representations of technology to very complex ones. In some ways this is bad (it took me a super long time, for instance, to come up with a simulable implementation that I was happy with) but it’s useful for studying different aspects of technological search. Let’s look at a few different implementations of a PTOP model and see what we find.
A level 1 PTOP model
Let’s start with an extremely simple version of PTOP. In this version, we have 10 possible objects, each with two possible properties. The first property, P0, can take on any value from 1 to 10 and is inherent and unique to that object. You can think of this as the model having 10 different chemical elements, each taking on a different value of P0. The second property is size, which can also take on any value from 1 to 10, but is adjustable. So you can have a large object with P0 equal to 1 and size equal to 10, or a small object with P0 equal to 1 and size equal to 1. Overall there are 100 possible sorts of objects: 10 different object types, each of which can be 10 different sizes.
This version of the model has four phenomena in total. Each phenomenon is triggered when the right two objects are connected, and the first of those objects (what we’ll call the input object) has the correct size. When the phenomenon is triggered, it adds a specific property to the second object (what we’ll call the output object). So in the image below, when an object with a P0 value of 1 and size 5 is connected to an object with a P0 value of 2, it triggers a phenomenon, which adds a new property, P1, to the second object.
The phenomena in this model are arranged in a hierarchy: triggering each phenomenon requires an object with the property added by the previous phenomenon. So to trigger the phenomenon that adds P2, you need an object with the P1 property. P3, in turn, requires an object with P2, and so on. You can think of this hierarchy of phenomena as representing something like “to trigger incandescence, I need an object with a high temperature. To achieve high temperature, I need to use the phenomenon of Joule heating, which I can trigger with the right sort of electric current. To create electric current, I need …” and so on.
In this version of the model, the goal is to create an object with the “final” property of P4. You can think of this as representing something like “light with the proper brightness” or “lead shot with the proper size and sphericity.” This can be done by creating the exact right arrangement of objects: five objects arranged in a line, each with the correct P0 property and size.
This is a very simple implementation of PTOP, which we’ll call a “level 1 model.” But it does capture a few things about the technological search process. First, the search space in even this very simple model is very large: 10 object types, 10 sizes, and 5 objects total means (10x10)^5 = 10 billion possible arrangements to produce a P5-level phenomenon.1 If you increased that to 100 objects, 100 sizes, and 10 different phenomena, you’d have 10^40 possible options. If we added more property types (maybe objects can have the properties of “temperature” and “density” in addition to size) the numbers would quickly become beyond astronomical.
But this simple version also shows the power that information can bring to bear on a large search space. When we looked at Arthur’s circuit search, we noted that what made the search tractable was modularity — finding a working design for a subcomponent, then locking that modular design into the system and using it as a repeatable ‘primitive’ element for further combinations. By preventing you from having to get every single part of a design correct in one shot, modularity effectively screens off many possibilities and reduces the size of the search space that must be traversed. As we found in that simulation:
A useful way of thinking about our 68 NAND gate search is that it’s like a huge, branching tree. At every step — every time we add a gate — there are thousands of branches, each one representing one possible way to wire up the gate. Each branch then splits into thousands more (representing all the possible ways of wiring up the next gate), which split into thousands more, which split into thousands more, until at the end we have 2^852 possible “leaves,” each one representing a unique way of wiring up all 68 gates. Trying to get all 68 gates right at once, and then checking to see whether or not you did, is like examining one single leaf, one path from the base of the tree all the way to the tip of a branch. Not only are you overwhelmingly likely to guess wrong, but you haven’t narrowed down your possibilities at all: all you know is that one single leaf wasn’t the right answer, leaving you with the rest of the 2^852 possible leaves to sift through.
Checking to see whether each gate we add is correct before we proceed to the next one, by contrast, massively narrows down the number of possibilities. Whenever we determine a gate isn’t in the right spot, it eliminates every possibility that branches off from that point. If there are 1000 possible ways to wire each gate, each time we guess correctly we’ve narrowed down the possibilities downstream of that choicepoint by 99.9%. Huge swaths of possibilities get eliminated at each correct guess, letting us converge on the correct answer much more quickly.
We can see these same basic mechanics with the PTOP model. With 10 object types, 10 sizes, 4 phenomena, and 1 billion effective possibilities, it takes (on average) 1 billion attempts to guess the entire correct design in one shot by randomly generating possible technologies.
But if we do a modular search — randomly adding just one object while randomly adjusting the size of the previous object until we’ve triggered the next phenomenon, then locking that successful design in and moving on — the search becomes much faster, because we’ve replaced a single billion-possibility space with a series of 100-possibility spaces. It takes on average 1,300 attempts to find the 10 type, 10 size, 4 phenomena answer, and even astronomically enormous technology space search problems become tractable.
This version also shows that the degree of modularity makes a huge difference in how easy a technology is to find. The more modules we have whose design we can lock in, the shorter each step is up the ladder to the working technology, and the easier each step is to take. If we take our 10 object type, 10 size model up to 100 phenomena levels, we’re now at an enormous 10^200 search space, but with 100 steps up the ladder that we can lock in, finding it is trivial — a random search finds it after about 10,000 attempts on average. The same-sized search space generated from 10 phenomena levels but 10 billion possible object types and sizes (which only gives us 10 steps up the ladder, rather than 100) becomes utterly impossible to find randomly, even with modular search.
This version of the model also lets us see how different sorts of knowledge can make the search process easier. For instance, as Joel Mokyr notes in The Gifts of Athena, scientific knowledge is very useful when trying to create some new technology, because “the range of experimentation possibilities that needs to be searched over is far larger if the searcher knows nothing about the natural principles at work.” In our level 1 PTOP model, scientific knowledge would be something like “phenomenon 3 can’t work with object type 2” or “phenomenon 4 must have its two objects of equal size.”
The usefulness of this sort of scientific knowledge is a function of how many possibilities it screens off. The more possibilities it screens off, the more bits of information it provides, and the more useful it is. So something like “phenomenon 5 can’t use object 1” or “object 3 can’t touch object 4” provides a relatively small amount of information, because it doesn’t eliminate that many possibilities. Knowledge of the sort “phenomenon 4 MUST use object 1” or “object 3 MUST touch object 4,” by contrast, screens off a lot more possibilities, provides much more information, and narrows the search much more effectively.
One reason that, in the real world, the technological development process is tractable is that a lot of our knowledge is of the latter type. Phenomena typically have specific triggering conditions, which we can observe and discover: Marconi knew what was needed to create electromagnetic waves when he was working on his radio, Edison knew what was needed to create incandescence in a lamp filament, and the scientists on the Manhattan Project knew roughly what conditions were needed to trigger a nuclear chain reaction.
A level 2 PTOP model
Even this highly simplified version of the PTOP model is useful for exploring various technological search dynamics. But ultimately it’s a little too simple to capture many of the more interesting dynamics of technological search. So let’s add some complexity. First, real phenomena often require multiple “input” objects, rather than just one: triggering the phenomenon of “combustion” in a gasoline engine requires fuel, an oxidizer, and an electric spark. So we’ll make it so that each phenomenon can have multiple input objects instead of just one. Second, there are often multiple different phenomena that you can use to accomplish some particular goal: if you want to make mechanical motion, for instance, there are a variety of different phenomena you can harness to do that, and motors built to harness them — electric motors, hydraulic motors, internal combustion engines — all work in different ways. So let’s also make it so that instead of just one phenomenon for each level, there can be more than one, each one requiring a different set of objects with the right properties to trigger.
With the level 1 PTOP model, there was only a single workable version of the technology. With the level 2 model, there are multiple working designs. And unlike the straight lines of objects of the previous model, this one creates branching, treelike chains.
With this version of the model (which I’ll call the “level 2 model”), even though there are a large number of possible working designs, the number of nonworking technologies is vastly larger, and finding a workable option by pure blind search quickly becomes unworkable.
We can solve this with a slightly different flavor of modular search, very similar to the “encapsulation” that Arthur uses in his technological evolution paper. In this version, the model starts out by randomly combining different objects with different properties, connected in different ways. Whenever an arrangement of objects triggers some phenomena, that arrangement gets bundled into a new object, and then that object can be chosen by the simulation to be randomly combined with other objects. As with our previous, simpler modular search, this lets the simulation accumulate partial solutions and quickly find working technologies even amidst very large search spaces.
A level 2 PTOP model can also be used to show the information-accumulating power of sexual reproduction. In a previous essay, we noted that sexual reproduction is its own sort of modular search — by letting children inherit genes from two parents, sex allows useful genetic “discoveries” made by many different lineages to spread throughout the population. This is in contrast to asexual reproduction, where only one particular lineage ultimately survives, and discoveries made by others die out due to a phenomenon called “clonal interference.” This allows sexually reproducing populations to converge on maximum fitness much more quickly.
We can see this same thing using the level 2 PTOP model. I ran a version of it with two different technology “populations.” Each population had 1,000 randomly generated technologies in it. In one population, I implemented asexual reproduction — each generation, every technology would get one random mutation to an object (deleting an object, adding an object, or changing an objects properties). The fittest members of the population, measured by the highest phenomena level they had unlocked, survived into the next generation. In the other population, I implemented sexual reproduction — in addition to random mutation, children would be generated by randomly crossing over the branches of two parents. With 5 levels of phenomena, asexual reproduction couldn’t achieve the maximum phenomena level after 2,000 generations in the example below; sexual reproduction, by contrast, found it after just over 100 generations.
A level 3 PTOP model
This flavor of PTOP is a little richer and can show a broader array of technological search dynamics, but it’s still a little simple, so let’s add some more complexity.
First, instead of making triggered properties — P1, P2, P3, etc. — binary (on or off), let’s make them be able to take on multiple values: before the property is switched on, it has a value of 0, while once a phenomenon triggers it, it can have a value from 1 to 10. We’ll make the value that it takes a function of two things: the size of the input object(s) and the value of the predecessor phenomenon. So for a phenomenon that triggers P2, the value of P2 will depend on the value of P1 and the size of its object. You can think of this as representing something like “the temperature in the lightbulb filament depends on the properties of the electric current flowing through it”: more amperage, or higher voltage, means higher filament temperatures. The brightness of the light emitted, in turn, will be a function of the temperature value of the filament.
We’ll make the value of triggered phenomena be determined in one of two ways. Either it’s maximized when the predecessor phenomenon and object size are EQUAL, or maximized when they’re as different as possible. So P2 can either be 10 when P1 and its size are the same (both 1, both 2, both 3), or when one is 10 and the other is 1. (For phenomena triggered by multiple input objects, we’ll take the average of the value calculated for each object.) We’ll call this version of the PTOP model the “level 3 model.”
This change actually makes the initial stage of the technological search much easier. Because the correct object size is no longer needed to trigger a phenomenon (just the correct object type), getting a technology that triggers the final phenomenon is now very easy (though it would be easy to change this by making the value of triggered phenomena dependent on some new property instead of size, and keeping whether or not a phenomenon is triggered size dependent). But now there’s an element of performance tuning. A technology that works, in the sense that it has a positive value for the final triggered phenomenon, might be quick to find, but to maximize performance — achieve a final phenomenon with a value of 10 — you need to keep iterating, fiddling with the sizes of the various objects to gradually push performance up.
This dialing-in step is meant to capture the technological development process: taking some technology that already works to some degree and pushing its performance higher or building a version that works in a particular way. With Edison’s lightbulb, for instance, incandescent bulbs had been demonstrated since the early 19th century, but their performance was poor — they burned out quickly, or the interior of the bulb blackened, or they used too much power. Edison took a technology whose configuration had been mostly figured out — a high-melting-point filament, a glass bulb, and an atmosphere to minimize reactivity were all common characteristics of previous bulbs — and pushed its performance higher by tweaking the properties of the various elements: the level of vacuum, the size of the filament, the exact type of carbon, and so on.
In the level 2 model, we had multiple phenomena for each level — multiple different ways to trigger P2, for instance. In the level 3 model, we’ll keep the same feature, but we’ll add a twist: different phenomena have different ranges for triggered properties that they can possibly achieve. So one way of triggering P2 might only be able to reach a value of 7, while the other might be able to achieve a value of 10. For some technologies, this might be fine; in other cases, maximizing performance will require using some other, different phenomena instead.
This also mirrors what we see with real-world technologies. When developing some new technology, the designer will be confronted with many possible ways of doing some particular job, and depending on the performance required, different options might work best. In the lightbulb, the performance of a carbon filament could only be pushed so high, and so eventually lightbulbs switched to tungsten filaments, which in turn required inventing a new process for producing ductile tungsten wire. Similarly, there are a variety of different ways of implementing the valves on an internal combustion engine to let gases into and out of the cylinders. Achieving very high engine performance, such as the number of revolutions per minute required on a Formula One car, requires complex valves that use things like compressed air instead of conventional wire springs, while if you’re building a four-door sedan the cheaper and simpler wire spring is fine.
Let’s now add one more element to the level 3 model. Up until now, we’ve had one single chain of properties: one phenomenon triggers another, which triggers another, and so on. Now let’s add a parallel set of properties, triggered by a parallel set of phenomena. In our lightbulb example, we can think of this as the temperature of the filament triggering not only incandescence but thermal expansion and thermionic emission.
(In this example, all these phenomena are triggered by the same property, temperature. In our model, for ease of modeling purposes we’ll have each of the parallel phenomena triggered by its own property.)
These parallel phenomena are triggered under the same conditions as the primary phenomena, but their values might not necessarily be determined in the same way: the conditions that create a value of 10 for P2 might create a value of 5, or 1, for parallel property T2. Ultimate performance of a technology will be a function of both of the final triggered properties: the value of, say, not just P9 but T9 as well.
This addition has a few consequences. For one, the technological search becomes more difficult: trying to dial in a technology by adjusting sizes randomly takes many more iterations if you’re trying to maximize both P9 and T9 than it does if you’re just trying to maximize one or the other. This mirrors technology more generally: the more dimensions of performance you care about, the more difficult getting a technology that’s good enough is.
Another consequence of this addition is that we now have design trade-offs. With multiple phenomena (and parallel phenomena) at each level, we can have different designs, which might achieve different levels of performance. I ran a level 3 search that generated random technological prototypes, and then tried to dial in the performance of each one for several different performance goals: maximizing P7 and T7, minimizing them, and achieving some specific value for each. At the end of the run, each goal had a fundamentally different arrangement, with different values for object sizes. The same basic technology was best implemented in different ways, depending on the performance goal.
Conclusion
To understand the nature of technological progress, it’s useful to think of creating a new technology as a sort of search process, one that’s made tractable by the intelligent acquisition and application of information. We can understand technological progress, in turn, by studying the nature of search processes — what sort of things make them easy, what sort of things make them hard, what sort of information acquisition methods we can bring to bear, and so on. The PTOP models described above are, I think, a useful tool for exploring these technological search dynamics: they’re simple to simulate, they’re flexible, and they can capture a lot of real-world elements of technological development.
The actual search space is 1 billion, not 10, because the size of the last object doesn’t affect any phenomena.

articles.title: ‘It’s a mistake’: reactions from tech leaders on Jensen Huang’s resignation
articles.body:
Nvidia announced this morning that Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO following reports of two affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy and one with a direct report. The situation surrounding Huang has unfolded quickly, with The New York Times only reporting on Friday that Huang and the suspected spy were “close” before other dominoes started to fall, leading to a swift fall from grace for one of the biggest names in technology. (Hours after Huang’s resignation was announced, Reuters reported that he also had an “intimate relationship” with another Nvidia employee.)
‘It’s a mistake’: reactions from tech leaders on Jensen Huang’s resignation
Many prominent voices in technology and the president of the US have publicly supported the former Nvidia CEO despite his ouster.
Prominent voices in technology have come out in support of Huang, with some calling the resignation a “waste” and a sad day for “all humanity.” The narrative among those leaders on X, at least, is that Huang’s resignation was rushed — perhaps an overreaction to salacious news stories about his personal life. Some others have had a more neutral reaction, commenting more on Huang’s achievements at the company’s helm. You can see a collection of those responses below.
President Donald Trump
“NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!”, Trump said on Truth Social.
Elon Musk, SpaceX and Tesla CEO
Elon Musk said in a reply to an X user that it would “be an honor” to hire Huang. He also replied to a post that said “You’d think we’d have learned from Steve Jobs and Travis Kalanick that one does not just simply replace the founder…” by saying “True words.”
Tim Sweeney, Epic Games CEO
Sweeney said that today is “A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction.”
Ahead of Huang’s resignation, Sweeney posted about how Huang “saved” a GDC 2015 presentation by dropping off a graphics card and said that “The dude truly is the visionary driver of the future of tech from the gaming GPU era to CUDA to AI supercomputers.”
Palmer Luckey, Anduril founder
“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said last night, before Huang’s resignation was announced.
Matt Mullenweg, Automattic co-founder and CEO
Mullenweg reposted an X post that followed his brief September ouster as CEO: “Founder advice: If you don’t have a coup attempt every few years, you’re not hiring strong enough leaders.” He said, “Just putting this back out there, for no reason whatsoever.”
David Heinemeier Hansson, 37signals CTO and creator of the Omarchy Linux distribution
“What a waste,” Hansson said this morning, replying to his own post from hours before: “NVIDIA would be wrong to fire Jensen. His marital indiscretions are between him, his wife, and a reprimand from the board. Have some proportionality.”
Clément Delangue, co-founder and CEO of Hugging Face (which Nvidia recently acquired for almost $13 billion)
“This whole thing sucks, and I wish none of it had happened,” Delangue said. “It’s a really sad day! But I want to make one thing clear: we’ll keep fighting for open-source AI, harder than ever. This is too important to slow down now. Let’s go!
Changpeng Zhao, former Binance CEO
“It’s a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign,” Zhao said.
Peter Steinberger, OpenClaw creator and OpenAI employee
“If that Spy’s goal was to destabilize one of the most successful American companies, they achieved their goal,” Steinberger said. “Ousting Jensen feels rushed and not right.” (“I agree,” replied Sweeney.)
Aravind Srinivas, Perplexity co-founder and CEO
Srinivas thanked Huang for “33 years of bold leadership” in a post this morning. “You built a small startup into America’s most valuable company, with relentless improvement. Your grit and perseverance should always be remembered. Your personal generosity with time and advice to founders like me has secured a bright future for America and AI.”
Jason Calacanis, All-In Podcast host
Calacanis reposted Trump’s post, tagging Tim Cook and telling him to “Keep the seat warm” for Huang while “the investigation is sorted out” and saying that “America needs you Mr. Cook.” Last night, he also said that Nvidia shareholders should “decide Jensen’s fate after the investigation is complete — not the press or online mobs.”
Lex Fridman, Lex Fridman Podcast host
In a post talking about how he has seen Huang show “kindness, humility, care to everyone around him,” Fridman said that “I’m in shock frankly at all of this, including the mass hysteria around it. I love America, and I think NVIDIA letting Jensen go is terrible for America. I stand with Jensen.”

articles.title: Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says
articles.body:
Microsoft's Global Outage May Be Worse Than Amazon's Or Crowdstrike's, Expert Says (arstechnica.com) 9
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: A global outage taking down a wide range of Microsoft 365 services remains ongoing Friday morning. The outage started midday Thursday, impacting users of Microsoft email, cloud, and AI services. Microsoft has documented the full list of services impacted by the error, while moving early Friday morning to protect customers around the world from losing emails during the extended disruptions. "Recovery actions are ongoing," the Microsoft 365 Status account confirmed on X. "To help preserve delayed mail during this event, we've extended email timeout to 48 hours."
Similar to recent world-shaking outages of widely used tech like Amazon Web Services and CrowdStrike, the Microsoft disruption looks like "one of the biggest outages of all time," Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, told NBC News. Possibly even "worse," he suggested.
Businesses, hospitals, police departments, and schools were among those scrambling to work around the outage. In Japan, it disrupted government IT infrastructure, according to deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki. NBC's report documented various harms, noting that "few public bodies were immune from the outage." In some cases, doctors couldn't send patients "important" updates on medication changes or follow-up care. The financial sector suffered, too, with people blocked from making bank transfers since they couldn't receive verification codes.
Justice systems were also hobbled. The Supreme Court in the Philippines saw its legal work derailed, NBC reported. And one US sheriff's office in Colorado reported that the outage made it difficult for people to post bond for prisoners' immediate release. It's unclear how many users were affected, but Microsoft estimated in January that the total number of paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions exceeded 450 million. Microsoft's most recent updates confirmed that it's seeing "broader improvements in North America, sustained improvements across much of Europe, and encouraging recovery signals in Asia Pacific."
"Some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as mitigation continues across remaining affected infrastructure," Microsoft said. "Our focus remains on stabilizing recovered infrastructure, completing mitigation in remaining impacted areas, and reducing delayed email queues and backlogs while we validate service consistency across connection methods."

articles.title: Whoop Launches a Social Network Where Every User Has a 'Verified Heartbeat'
articles.body:
Whoop Launches a Social Network Where Every User Has a 'Verified Heartbeat' (theverge.com) 35
			
		 	
				Whoop has launched Humans, a social network built into its fitness app where every account is a real person with a "verified heartbeat." The wearable company claims its platform is "entirely human," unlike other social media platforms that are "saturated with artificial intelligence, automated accounts and bots, and manufactured content." The Verge reports:  Starting Thursday, Whoop members can share their data from its wearables on the app's new Whoop Humans social network. Users can make their metrics, activities, and achievements visible to other Whoop wearers, post Story-like "Moments" with photos and captions, and add comments and reactions on other members' posts. [...]
In the Community tab in Whoop's app, users can scroll through Moments from people they're following, like tapping through your Stories feed on Instagram but with your friends' fitness tracker data. In one of Whoop's examples, swiping up on a user's Moments post with a photo from their run shows a map with their route and details like their pace and distance. The Community tab also shows cards for people in your "community" with their sleep, recovery, and strain scores.
Whoop says users choose which activities, achievements, and metrics they want to share on Humans, including Recovery, Strain, Sleep, HRV, and resting heart rate. Any activities marked as sensitive aren't shared by default. There's also an option to keep Moments posts private and a "Stealth Mode" for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

Any activities marked as sensitive aren’t shared by default. There’s also an option to keep Moments posts private and a “Stealth Mode” for temporarily hiding health and performance data without changing your sharing settings.

articles.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
articles.body:
Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people.
Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. That includes Cornell University, Penn State University, Elgin Community College, Emory University, Binghamton University, Kent State University and the University of Wisconsin’s Madison, Milwaukee and Oshkosh branches. Last week, the University of Buffalo announced an indefinite pause on its plans for a 60-day pilot program.
Elgin Community College tried, unsuccessfully, to cancel its Flock contract before it expired in April. School officials said they resorted to placing black plastic trash bags over the cameras “out of an abundance of caution” until the company removed the cameras after the agreement lapsed.
A few schools – Appalachian State University and the University of North Carolina’s (UNC) Charlotte and Chapel Hill campuses – have kept Flock contracts but restricted national access to the cameras’ records. UNC Charlotte made the change after local news outlet WBTV found that the Houston police department had searched the school’s Flock camera network more than any other agency between March and May 2026: a total of 183,000 times.
Schools that haven’t yet restricted what agencies can access Flock or dropped contracts are feeling the pressure. At the University of Florida and Florida State University, activists have turned to protests, online campaigns and petitions to express their discontent. The state of Florida recently banned Flock cameras and other license plate readers from its highways, but those laws don’t extend to private property or local rights-of-way.
The uproar on campuses reflects a broader uprising. This year, dozens of cities have deactivated, canceled or rejected Flock contracts. Vigilantes have damaged and destroyed the devices to the delight of their social media followers.
Flock Safety said in an emailed statement that its cameras help solve crimes and increase public safety by giving campus police credible leads. The company highlighted cases in which local law enforcement said Flock cameras helped track down a shooter at Brown University, arrest a person who shot a gun in the parking lot of a high school in Colorado and find a suspect in an investigation about more than $100,000 in stolen equipment from an on-campus construction site at UNC Charlotte.
“We understand that schools and universities must evaluate public safety technology, and we respect each institution’s authority to make those decisions, but taking away these tools could impact the safety of students,” the company said in an emailed statement.
Flock also denies that its cameras fuel mass surveillance and that it partners with federal immigration authorities, although news reports have documented indirect ways that local police have used the network to help US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. This summer, Flock also introduced updated policies around auditing, as well as data retention and sharing.
Flock out, new cameras in
Student protesters are confronting many of the same challenges organizers in cities that have dropped Flock have faced: most commonly, a pivot to license plate readers from other vendors.
Stanford is already installing replacement automatic license plate recognition (ALPRs) from the Canadian company, Genetec. Nguyen, the Stanford student, still counts the move away from Flock as a win but says there’s still work to be done, as student organizers’ goal is “to prevent any possibility of mass surveillance on campus”. She’s speaking with the university’s transportation department to push for transparency around who can access the data captured by the cameras.

Stanford did not respond to a request for comment but has said that Genetec, a Canadian company, will continue to store data on its internal servers for 30 days and that the new system is “designed for use within a single institution”. UW-Madison did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Binghamton University, Ryan Yarosh, said in an emailed statement that school officials have met with concerned faculty and students, and respects their “right to express their concerns”.

High schoolers are getting in on Flock activism, too.

His research led him to believe that the network is a dragnet that violates the fourth amendment. Aditya Manchanda and Henry Jones, who are part of their school’s Young Democratic Socialists of America chapter, made a video on TikTok about ALPRs and their petition attracted local news coverage.
“Schools should be a safe place, and we don’t feel safe,” Aditya said. “We feel our privacy being violated with the presence of these cameras.”
After gathering signatures, the duo emailed the school’s principal. “I know he wasn’t too pleased because we got media attention, and that’s not a great look,” Aditya said. articles.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off

articles.title: AI unlocks Gödel's notebooks, said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
articles.body:
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.
Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.
In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.
“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”
Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.
The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.
“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”
Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”
In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”
Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”
Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”
Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”

articles.title: Nvidia employees petition to bring back Jensen Huang
articles.body:
Some Nvidia employees are calling for Jensen Huang’s return even after his multiple reported extramarital affairs and abrupt resignation, according to internal correspondence reviewed by WIRED.
An internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime engineer at Nvidia urged the company’s board to take employee sentiment into consideration prior to taking any action. The submission has attracted more than 1,600 comments since then, with several asking board members to find a way to bring back Huang.
“If you believe in the mission, bring back THE boss,” wrote one anonymous commenter.
“We are all humans and can make mistakes. Jensen did so many good things and he needs a second chance,” wrote another.
One employee went as far as sending a companywide email demanding transparency into Huang’s exit. “I stand by Jensen,” the staffer wrote. “Not because I believe any person is infallible, but because I refuse to believe that standing for fairness must mean standing at a distance from someone whose leadership has meant so much to us.”
The employee couldn’t be reached for comment, while the engineer behind the suggestion box post declined to comment.
Nvidia and its new board chair, investor Harvey Jones, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.
Huang, a 63-year-old who had led Nvidia since its founding in 1993, wrote in an email to employees on Sunday that he had been “unfaithful to [his] wife” and that there was “no excuse.” The acknowledgement followed reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. The board announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday morning, following reports of an alleged second affair with a direct report. (This employee has not commented on the matter.) Since then, Reuters reported on an alleged affair with yet another Nvidia employee. Huang hasn’t commented about these reports since his Sunday email.
Nvidia’s board is largely made up of early Nvidia investors and Huang’s longtime confidants. It named Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO and appointed former Synopsys CEO Harvey Jones as chair of the board. The crisis has cost the company $1 trillion in market value since the allegations surfaced, prompted investigations from US lawmakers and the FBI, and raised the prospect of new export controls on chips.
It’s been business as usual inside the company throughout this week, but Huang’s resignation left many employees stunned. In the hours after, about two dozen employees posted on LinkedIn in support of Huang, with one describing their faith in his leadership as unwavering. Over the same period, WIRED couldn’t identify any posts from Nvidia employees in support of his resignation.
One employee who has been at Nvidia for a couple of years and wasn’t authorized to speak publicly says they perceive the desire for Huang’s reinstatement as widespread. They worry the company will eventually suffer without its founder at the helm and say that the board must bring him back. “Nvidia is Nvidia because of Jensen,” the employee tells WIRED.
Many employees had expected a board investigation to conclude before any big changes would occur. For instance, the suggestion-box post called on the board to share its findings with employees and formally solicit their sentiment “about Jensen’s continuing as our CEO.”
Instead, Huang left just as the inquiry had begun. Staffers are seeking to better understand why. “If America fails the man who helped build its future,” the employee in the companywide email stated, “then this world does not deserve Jensen Huang.”

articles.title: $11.4M in Nvidia hardware vanishes during shipment from CA to TX
articles.body:
Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments.
According to The Mercury News, the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations.
Oakland police confirm investigation
The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement:
“The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.”
The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded.
Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products
The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance.
In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding, from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case.
Why it matters
The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation.

Six pallets of NVIDIA computer hardware worth a reported $11.4 million disappeared during a shipment from California to Texas. A truck collected the merchandise in Oakland on Aug. 29 for delivery to Fort Worth. Investigators reportedly tracked the vehicle through several extended stops before losing its trail in Southern California. The Oakland Police Department confirmed an ongoing grand theft investigation following a complaint filed Sept. 13, 2026. The disappearance comes amid reports of nearly $111 million in stolen data center freight involving other high-value technology shipments.
According to The Mercury News, the vehicle displayed a food transportation company’s logo during the scheduled pickup. The driver subsequently traveled south, making several stops lasting multiple hours. Investigators eventually lost track of the truck in San Bernardino County. A separate $12 million cargo theft investigation involved suspects who allegedly exploited established trucking identities to obtain freight. Authorities have not linked the two investigations.
Oakland police confirm investigation
The Oakland Police Department provided FreightWaves with the following statement:
“The Oakland Police Department (OPD) is investigating a grand theft that occurred in East Oakland. The victim reported the crime to OPD on September 13, 2026. The investigation is ongoing, and anyone with information is asked to contact the OPD General Crimes Unit at (510) 238-3728.”
The Sept. 13 complaint date does not establish when the theft occurred. Police have not confirmed the reported $11.4 million valuation or identified the specific merchandise. Authorities also have not identified the cargo’s owner, shipper, motor carrier or driver. Investigators have not publicly explained the vehicle’s extended stops or established whether criminals impersonated a transportation provider. Police have not announced arrests or confirmed any recovery of the merchandise. FreightWaves contacted NVIDIA for comment and followed up, but the company has not responded.
Previous thefts involving NVIDIA products
The Oakland investigation follows other significant thefts involving NVIDIA merchandise in Northern California. During 2025, Fremont and Union City police investigated burglaries involving more than $7.5 million in NVIDIA products. Those incidents targeted valuable computer hardware at separate locations. Authorities have not established any connection between those investigations and the latest disappearance.
In a separate September incident, thieves stole two PlusAI trailers, including one displaying NVIDIA branding, from a Fremont, California, warehouse. The trailers contained approximately 40,000 pounds of sand rather than NVIDIA hardware. Police recovered both trailers in nearby Newark. Investigators have not established any connection between that theft and the Oakland case.
Why it matters
The reported disappearance of $11.4 million in NVIDIA hardware underscores the financial stakes of transporting high-value freight. Regardless of how this shipment disappeared, carrier verification, shipment visibility and communication remain critical throughout transportation.
Click here for more articles on cargo theft and freight fraud by Phil Brink.

CBP seizes 1,000-plus pounds of meth in produce truck at Texas border – FreightWaves
$500,000 SIG Sauer shipment stolen in fictitious pickup, two arrested in California – FreightWaves

articles.title: The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
articles.body:
Gone are the days when you could just buy your father a random tie or some leather-clad alcohol vessel or a shaving kit. Dads want — nay, deserve — something memorable. Luckily for you, it’s not that hard to find something special that he’ll approve of, and we’re here to guide you.
The Verge’s 2026 gift guide for dads
This year, why not get Dad a gift or two he won’t expect?
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
We’ve curated this year’s gift list with the modern father in mind, whether he’s a gamer, creator, chef, or simply a gadget lover. There’s a lot in here we think he’ll like, from noise-canceling headphones like the Sonos Ace Ultra and an autonomous drone to a brilliant QD-OLED monitor and a nifty light that’s perfect for illuminating his next campsite. Whatever your dad is into, we’ve got you covered.
Antigravity’s A1 is the ultimate gadget for the dad who dreams of owning the sky. The compact drone comes with specialized goggles that will make him feel like he’s in the cockpit, and it records always-on, 360-degree 8K video. It’s an exhilarating flight experience and an excellent creator’s tool in one slick package.
Dyson PencilVac Fluffycones
Cleaning gadgets like Dyson’s PencilVac FluffyCones are never cheap, but they’re often worth the cost and a pleasure to use. The lightweight, broom-replacing stick vacuum doesn’t do carpets, but its rolling bars pack incredible cleaning power for touching up hard floors, including stairs.
For those who love travel but hate the constraints of a hotel TV, Belkin’s ConnectAir is a slick solution. Plug the transmitter into any device with a USB-C video-out port and the receiver into the TV’s HDMI port, and voilà, you’re easily (and wirelessly) connected.
Sonos Ace Ultra
Sonos raised its headphones game on all fronts with the Ace Ultra, which deliver better noise canceling, improved sound, and the feature we’ve all been waiting for: Wi-Fi support. With the ability to bounce audio across your Sonos ecosystem, including from a TV via newer Sonos soundbars, Dad’s sonic sanctuary is finally complete.
Werewolf’s affordable dongle kit provides an almost magical way to power nearly any DC device from a USB-C charger or portable battery. Program it from a mobile app, connect it to your old gear, and everything from a PC monitor to an original Game Boy can accept USB-C charging.
Who would have thought a simple hook could make roaming the city with a backpack so much more convenient? After testing Peak Design’s well-designed bags, we’re convinced the clever addition is a game-changer for anyone who doesn’t want to leave their bag on the filthy ground.
WiiM’s first soundbar builds on its seamless Sonos-esque connectivity with a sleek design, detailed sound, and up-firing speakers for Dolby Atmos spatial audio. It also pairs with other speakers for surround sound through a no-fuss setup process, including ones you already own that are linked to one of WiiM’s amplifiers.
Alienware AW3426DW QD-OLED Gaming Monitor
Your dad needs an awesome monitor, but there are 10 billion options. Alienware’s 34-inch Penta Tandem QD-OLED delivers top-end picture quality, with vibrant colors and perfect blacks, plus a swift 280Hz refresh rate. Best of all, it’s not nearly as expensive as you might think.
If your dad is still reading books on his phone (or aging e-reader), it’s time for an upgrade. The latest in Amazon’s series of waterproof, auto-dimming e-readers loads books faster than the prior model and offers a slick aluminum upgrade. No matter which you choose, it’s a better way to bring the library along.
Sharge Disk Pro 2 SSD / HDMI dock
Give your father a little nostalgia and a lot of convenience in one package with this stylish USB-C dock and SSD combo gadget. The cassette-shaped Sharge Disk Pro 2 works as a hub with support for HDMI at 4K, SD and microSD card slots, USB-A and USB-C ports, along with up to 8TB of storage stored within.
Smart TVs are often pretty dumb. If your dad is always complaining about his TV, or if you want to get ahead of it, grab the latest Apple TV 4K. Although it’s not cheap, it stands out with built-in mics for Siri AI, lots of power, HomePod surround sound support, and a simple, ad-free interface.
The Switch 2 leverages the same ideas as its predecessor, only with a larger, 7.9-inch display, a faster chip, and a bevy of new social features. However, its most important trait is that it’s the newest Nintendo console, which means access to a host of weird, beautiful, family-friendly games that only Nintendo could dream up, now on a better screen.
Oura Ring 5
Oura didn’t reinvent the wheel with the Ring 5, but it did reshape it into a slimmer, thinner, more wearable design that could make all the difference. Inside are the same extensive health and fitness tracking features for charting everything from sleep to heart health, backed by long battery life.
The CS-Pro will make your dad feel like a private eye in the early ’80s. The retro-inspired digital camera serves up 16-megapixel stills and offers four filters accessible from its tactile dial, plus USB-C charging, a high-quality Xenon flash, and a 4GB SD card for plenty of vintage photo fun.
BougeRV T1 Portable Telescopic Camping Light
BougeRV’s fancy, compact lamp will spark joy for the glamper in your life, as well as everyone else. Its powerful, foldable spread of LEDs provides a blast of light anywhere plug-ins can’t reach, from the beach to the shed where that scary spider holds court, with up to 60 hours of light on low power.
The Rival Pro offers plenty of thoughtful extras, including swappable batteries and an ultra-wideband base station for a seamless, low-latency connection. The gaming mouse’s lightweight design and 8,000Hz polling rate also deliver both accurate and ergonomic performance for up to 16 hours per charge.
It’s time to help Dad ditch his collection of plastic reusable cups, which have clearly seen better days. NotNeutral’s hand-pressed, timeless tumbler offers ’70s vibes with a modern twist, making it the perfect vessel for whatever Dad twists into his favorite drink.
Give the gift that fixes past home improvement transgressions. These handy Japanese-made pliers from Vampire Tools have one fundamental purpose — to remove stripped screws — and they’re damn good at it. The best part? Watching Dad’s face light up seconds before he sprints to the garage for them.
One Piece Straw Hat Pirates Hockey Jersey
For the manga or live-action Netflix show lover on your list, this fashionable Pirates jersey, inspired by Monkey D. Luffy from the seminal pirate adventure series One Piece, will be as surprising as it is delightful.
If you’re after a cheap, useful stocking stuffer, Trond’s reliable three-prong extension cord is a practical pick that’s available in leftward or rightward configurations to fit nearly any outlet. Dad will probably say, “Oh, I’ve always wanted one of these,” and this time he’ll mean it.
Star Wars Zero Company
Zero Company, a strategy game set in the twilight of the Clone Wars, is a fun way to get lost in the Star Wars universe. The single-player, turn-based title lets players command a diverse team of characters across a gorgeous expanse of worlds, offering hours of solitary entertainment.
If your father already owns an Apple Watch, the Nomad Stratos is a foolproof upgrade idea. The refined watch band features titanium links with a rubbery interior for durable comfort, and it comes in an array of subtle color options that make it as suitable for the office as it is for the slopes.
Apple Crossbody Strap
We fell for Apple’s handy iPhone strap due to its effortless accessibility and comfy design, which uses flexible magnets to keep excess segments in check. From biking to hiking to concerts, it’s a great way to sling your iPhone 18 Pro, assuming you have a compatible phone case.
The new Fitbit Air provides the same great fitness tracking we’ve come to expect in a comfortable design that virtually disappears on your wrist. Google’s AI Coach can be overly assertive, but the tracker’s great battery life and metrics for everything from sleep to blood oxygen make it an excellent gift for anyone who needs a healthy hand.
Most of us have thousands of photos in the cloud, but if a photo never makes it into the real world, did it really happen? Existentialism aside, the Cricut StickerPix offers a new way to play with photos, providing you with everything you need to turn any picture into a pro-quality print or sticker.
SwitchBot Standing Circulator Fan
This battery-powered fan is a big upgrade over your average plug-in job. As a 3D circulator, it can tilt to push air in all directions. It can be controlled from an app and even detaches from its stand to sit on a desk or tabletop. Quiet, powerful, and versatile, it’s equipped for nearly any adventure on or off the grid.
Have you broken something fragile that seems impossible to mend? Maybe all you need is a Kintsugi Repair Kit, which provides the Japanese method and a special lacquer to repair and restore broken ceramics to good health. The resulting golden scar is merely to remind us that rebuilding is possible.
If your favorite cinephile is looking to get off the streaming carousel, the Kaleidescape Strato E is the key. The premium player lets library builders locally store and play their favorite films and TV shows in lossless 4K resolution with Dolby Atmos for sterling entertainment that’s all theirs.
Once The Great British Baking Show becomes an obsession, only a serious stand mixer will do for replicating recipes at home. This mixer’s timeless design adds new features in what KitchenAid calls its biggest upgrade since 1955, with a new half-speed setting and a control lever that lets you set speeds between its standard settings.
Instruo Pocket Scion Bio-Feedback Instrument
The Pocket Scion is unlike any musical instrument you’ve witnessed before, one that uses the “biofeedback” from plants to trigger built-in synths. The device offers MIDI-out to send digital signals to outboard synths, and it includes an app for both macOS and Windows, finally giving you a way to make your favorite fern a rockstar.
When it comes to jotting down notes, there’s nothing like a pen and paper. At least, that’s what we thought before we tried the Remarkable Paper Pure. Offering a strikingly realistic writing experience that saves everything in the digital realm, this tablet is a brilliant way to bridge the gap and save paper.
Fairphone 6 Plus
Electronics are becoming more sustainable, and Fairphone is leading the way. The Fairphone 6 Plus may seem like a regular Android phone on paper, but the ability to repair and replace its internals, from the screen to the battery, makes it anything but average.

If you need a whole new set of frying pans for your kitchen, don’t miss this Hybrid Fry Pan Set that’s 38% off. It includes an 8-inch, 10-inch, and 12-inch pan with coordinating lids. This set is perfect for cooking every day, and best of all, the pans are completely dishwasher-safe.
